title: Mofongo
subtitle: Puerto Rican fried green plantain mashed with garlic and pork crackling
excerpt: Fried green plantain pounded with garlic, olive oil and pork crackling into a dense, flavourful mash. This recipe serves 4 and takes about 40 minutes. Mofongo is one of the most iconic dishes of Puerto Rican cooking, shaped into a dome and served with broth or a stew poured around it.
sourceNotes: Mofongo has roots in the West African dish fufu, which enslaved people brought to Puerto Rico. The dish fuses African technique with plantain, a fruit introduced to the Americas from West Africa via the Canary Islands. Mofongo is now one of the most recognisable dishes of Puerto Rican cuisine.

recipe.temperatureNote: Oil should reach 175C for frying the plantain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Puerto Rican dish made from fried green plantain that is mashed with garlic and pork crackling in a pilon (mortar). It is typically shaped into a dome and served with broth or a meat stew poured over it.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 40 minutes.

is traditionally mashed in a large wooden pilon (mortar and pestle). A large stone or ceramic mortar works well. You can use a potato masher as a last resort but the texture will be less cohesive. The plantain must be green and unripe for this dish: ripe plantain is sweet and soft, while green plantain is starchy and firm, which gives mofongo its dense, satisfying texture.

Work in batches if your mortar is small. Mash each batch of fried plantain while it is still hot from the oil; cold plantain becomes stiff and hard to work with. Add the garlic, olive oil and crumbled chicharron as you go. The finished mofongo should be cohesive enough to hold a dome shape when pressed into a small bowl and inverted onto the plate.

items.prepNote: finely minced or pounded to a paste

content.text: Peel the green plantains. To peel green plantain easily, cut off both ends, score the skin lengthways with a knife, and pry the skin off in sections. Cut the plantain into rounds about 2.5cm thick.

Heat vegetable oil to 175C in a deep pan. Fry the plantain rounds in batches for 4 to 5 minutes until cooked through but not yet golden. They should be just tender. Remove and drain on kitchen paper. Do not cook them until fully brown at this stage.

While the plantain is still hot, place several pieces into the mortar along with a portion of the minced garlic, 2 tbsp olive oil and 100g crumbled chicharron (pork crackling). Pound and mash firmly until the mixture comes together into a cohesive mass. Season generously with salt.
Divide the mofongo into 4 portions. Press each into a small bowl to shape it into a dome, then invert onto a plate.

Pour hot chicken or beef stock around the mofongo dome. The broth softens the outside as you eat. Serve with a squeeze of lime. Mofongo can also be served with a stew (carne guisada or shrimp in garlic sauce work well) spooned around it.

attrs.symptom: Mofongo is dry and crumbly and will not hold its shape
attrs.cause: Not enough fat added during mashing, or the plantain was too cold
attrs.fix: Drizzle in more olive oil a teaspoon at a time and pound again. Make sure you mash the plantain while it is still hot from the fryer.

attrs.symptom: Plantain is hard and starchy even after frying
attrs.cause: Plantain was not cooked for long enough at the frying stage
attrs.fix: The first fry should cook the plantain through until a skewer passes easily. If they are still very hard, return to the oil for 2 to 3 more minutes before mashing.

attrs.cause: Oil temperature was too low and the plantain absorbed oil instead of frying crisp
attrs.fix: Check the oil is at 175C before adding the plantain. Drain well on kitchen paper after frying. Blotting with more kitchen paper before mashing also helps.

content.text: Mofongo is Puerto Rico's most recognised dish outside the island. In San Juan it is served in restaurants from lunch through to late night, with countless variations of what gets served alongside: garlic shrimp, braised beef, fried pork, or simply a bowl of chicken broth. The pilon used to make it is a cultural object as well as a kitchen tool, and many Puerto Rican families have one passed down through generations.
